title: Sultanate of Sambas
capsule: The Sultanate of Sambas was a Malay Muslim state on the northwestern coast of Borneo, traditionally founded in 1609 by Raden Sulaiman, who took the name Muhammad Shafi ud-din I upon conversion. Its location on the Sambas River made it a hub for gold and pepper trade linking Borneo's interior to Chinese and Malay mercantile networks. Dutch VOC commercial pressure escalated into military intervention in the early nineteenth century, and the Netherlands formally brought Sambas under colonial authority in 1819. The sultanate retained ceremonial existence until Indonesian independence, with its territory constituted as Sambas Regency.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core political history is reasonably documented in Dutch colonial records and Malay chronicles, but precise territorial boundaries for the pre-Dutch period are poorly attested.
